title: the Sri Sukta
hook: a letter that starts 'to whom it may concern' and ends with a name: the line where the hymn stops saying 'her' and says 'you'

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sri Sukta painted her portrait: smiling, moist and blazing, satisfied and satisfying. Whose plate or cup did you fill? Today, the hymn turns to face her. Day one thousand ninety-five.

A cover letter begins: to whom it may concern. Polite, careful, written to a title. Three paragraphs later, if the job matters enough, it starts to sound like a person talking to a person. A speech at a retirement party can go the same way: it starts about the colleague, and ends turned toward her, glass up, speaking to her directly. Something like that happens in the Sri Sukta today. For several lines the singer has talked about the goddess. Called her near. Described her. Then, at the end of one line, the pronoun changes.
screen: `TO WHOM IT MAY CONCERN.` → `A PERSON TALKING TO A PERSON.` → `THE PRONOUN CHANGES.`

segments.voice: Here's the line, in paraphrase. Bright as the moon, shining, blazing with glory, Sri, cherished by the gods, generous: I take refuge in her, the lotus one. May misfortune be gone from me. I choose you. Walk through it slowly. The first half is still the portrait: moonlight, glory, generosity. Then a step closer. I take refuge in her. Refuge is a strong word. It's what you look for when the weather turns, or when you've run out of ways to manage on your own. The singer isn't only admiring her now. He's placing himself under her shelter. Then the request: may misfortune be gone from me. The hymn's word for misfortune is Alakshmi, and she'll come back later in the hymn with a face of her own. For now, she's simply what the singer wants gone. And then the last two words. Tvam vrine. I choose you. All along it's been she, her, Sri. Suddenly it's you. The singer turns and speaks to her face to face. And the verb is choose: the kind of word a person might use for choosing a partner, or a guide. Not I want your gold. I choose you. Some readers hear in that turn the heart of the whole hymn: underneath the cattle and the gold, the singer is choosing the goddess herself. Others keep the plain sense close: a person in trouble, asking for shelter and for hard luck to end. Both can be true in one breath. People in trouble still choose whom to turn to.
screen: `MOONLIGHT, GLORY, GENEROSITY.` · `I TAKE REFUGE IN HER.` · `MAY MISFORTUNE BE GONE.` · `SHE BECOMES YOU.` · then, large: `I CHOOSE YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: turn toward. Settle, and let the breath slow. Bring to mind something that's been weighing on you, a stretch of bad luck, a worry you keep circling. Let it be there. Then ask yourself, gently: where do I go for shelter? A person, a place, a practice, a prayer. Don't judge the answer. Just notice it, and turn toward it in your mind, the way the hymn turns from her to you. If you pray, you can speak to the goddess, or to God, directly, in your own words. If you don't, simply rest under whatever shelter you found. The bell holds the time.
The Sri Sukta. The hymn where the singer takes refuge in Sri, asks for misfortune to go, and turns to say: I choose you.
Your line: the Sri Sukta. Today, instead of talking about someone who shelters you, talk to them: one message, one call, one sentence. Day one thousand ninety-five.

howItsDone: Some Hindus recite the Sri Sukta in full during Lakshmi worship at home or in temples, so this verse of refuge is spoken as part of the whole hymn.

at the end of this line he turns and says: I choose you.

fork.setup: you've been describing the goddess line after line, always as 'her'. now you're in trouble and need shelter. what do you do?
options: keep describing her, politely, from a distance.
turn and speak to her: I choose you.
ask the fire to carry the message for you.
fork.reveal: the singer takes refuge in her, asks for misfortune to go, and then turns: tvam vrine, I choose you. the pronoun changes from her to you.

original.note: Sanskrit: tvāṃ vṛṇe, 'I choose you,' the last words of this line of the Sri Sukta.

trapdoor: what you thought: a hymn about getting things.
what it means: at its turn the singer takes refuge in Sri and says I choose you, speaking to her directly.
what a scholar hears: śaraṇam ahaṃ prapadye, alakṣmīr me naśyatāṃ, tvāṃ vṛṇe: refuge, the end of misfortune, and a shift from third person to second.
recall: a warrior, and a daughter coming home
the year just walked and kept

sources.ref: Sri Sukta, verse 5 (Rig Veda khila, as commonly recited)

notes: Verse 5 paraphrased: candrāṃ prabhāsāṃ yaśasā jvalantīṃ śriyaṃ loke devajuṣṭām udārām / tāṃ padminīm īṃ śaraṇam ahaṃ prapadye alakṣmīr me naśyatāṃ tvāṃ vṛṇe. Confirm 'cherished by the gods' for devajuṣṭām and 'generous' for udārām.

The claim that this is where the hymn first shifts to direct address ('the pronoun changes') should be checked against verses 1–4: verse 1 and 2 address Jatavedas (Agni) in the vocative, not Sri; verses 3–4 speak of Sri in the third person. Confirm 'for several lines the singer has talked about the goddess'.

vṛṇe glossed 'I choose'; the comparison to choosing a partner or a guide is an image, not a lexical claim (the verb is used of choosing a bride/groom and of choosing a priest in Vedic usage). Confirm.
Reading of the verse as the hymn's heart is attributed to 'some readers'; confirm.

Editor pass: the hook's wedding toast swapped for a retirement-party speech (day 1093's hook is a wedding procession); 'it's the same kind of word you'd use for choosing a partner' softened to an English image so it doesn't read as a claim about Sanskrit usage.
